summary:
NDVI compares near-infrared with red reflectance: healthy vegetation reflects strongly in the near-infrared and absorbs red. It returns NDVI, EVI approximation, estimated fractional cover and surface class (0 water … 6 very dense), and the panel shows all of them at once.

The result runs from −1 to +1 and is the most widely used satellite index of vegetation vigour. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index)
sections.html:
NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red)

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
NIRnear-infrared reflectance0–1
Redred reflectance0–1
NDVInormalised difference vegetation index−1 to 1

sections.title: How do I use the NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index)?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: near-infrared reflectance of 0.42, red reflectance of 0.08.

Substituting them into the formula gives ndvi of 0.68, evi approximation of 0.4474, estimated fractional cover of 79.34%, surface class (0 water … 6 very dense) of 5.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
−1 to 0 (class 0)Water, snow, cloudno vegetation signal
0 – 0.1 (class 1)Barrenrock, sand, built-up
0.1 – 0.2 (class 2)Sparsebare soil with scattered plants
0.2 – 0.4 (class 3)Shrub and early cropdry grassland
0.4 – 0.6 (class 4)Moderate canopygrowing crop
0.6 – 0.8 (class 5)Denseclosed canopy at peak season
0.8 – 1 (class 6)Very denserainforest or irrigated crop at full cover

  • NDVI saturates in dense canopies: above a leaf area index of about 3 it stops rising, which is why EVI was developed.

  • Atmospheric haze and thin cloud lower NDVI without changing the ground; compositing several dates reduces that.

  • Values are only comparable when computed from the same sensor and the same processing baseline — an NDVI from Landsat and one from Sentinel-2 need harmonising.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Mixing reflectance scaled 0–255 with reflectance scaled 0–1.
  • Comparing a growing-season maximum with an off-season image.
  • Reading NDVI as biomass in a saturated canopy.

faq.q: Why is NDVI negative over water?
faq.a: Water absorbs near-infrared much more strongly than red, so NIR − Red goes negative.

faq.q: What does the NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns NDVI, EVI approximation, estimated fractional cover and surface class (0 water … 6 very dense). Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
